idiom_name: compact JWS via JJWT, stored in a cookie or sent as a bearer token
implementation_notes: The idiomatic Java realization of this pattern is a signed JWT: JJWT builds a compact JWS whose claims carry the conversation state (subject, cart, tenant, scopes) and whose signature makes the token tamper-evident, so any instance can validate it without a lookup; the token travels in a cookie for browser clients or in the Authorization header for API clients. Choose it when the state must be understood by other stacks, when the carrier is a header rather than a cookie, or when a short exp is enough of a lifecycle. JJWT also provides JWE when the payload must stay confidential. The alternative variant exists for teams that refuse a JWT dependency or need the state hidden inside an opaque cookie; a signed-only token is readable by the client, so never put PII in its claims.
code_sketch:
String token = Jwts.builder()
    .subject(user.id())
    .claim("cart", items)
    .expiration(Date.from(Instant.now().plus(Duration.ofMinutes(30))))
    .signWith(signingKey)
    .compact();

Claims claims = Jwts.parser().verifyWith(signingKey).build()
    .parseSignedClaims(request.getCookieValue("sid"))
    .getPayload();
pitfalls: Algorithm confusion and unverified parsing: always pin the expected algorithm/key when parsing, and never accept a token just because it decodes.
A JWT is a client-held snapshot: there is no revocation list, so exp must be short and key rotation is the only global logout.
Cookie-borne JWTs inherit the ~4 KB cookie limit; header-borne ones do not, but then the client must be an API consumer rather than a browser.
Clock skew and exp validation are the server's responsibility - a stale token replayed after logout is still valid until it expires.

variants.name: Opaque encrypted cookie (Jakarta Cookie API + JCA AES-GCM)
variants.idiom_name: Cookie + Cipher AES/GCM/NoPadding and Mac HmacSHA256 over a serialized session record
variants.implementation_notes: When the state must be opaque to the client and no token format is wanted, the servlet layer provides the carrier (Cookie with setHttpOnly/setSecure/setPath/setMaxAge) and the JDK provides the cryptography: serialize the session, encrypt it with Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding") under a per-record IV and a stable key, print the sealed record into the cookie value, and on the next request decrypt before deserializing; Mac with HmacSHA256 is the alternative when only tamper detection is needed. This variant suits intranet or single-stack deployments that already manage keys, and it keeps the wire format entirely private. Prefer the JWT variant when other services must read the token.
pitfalls: Cookie values must obey the cookie grammar: no whitespace, commas, semicolons or equals signs, which is why the record is base64url-encoded before it is written.
Never reuse an AES-GCM IV under the same key; generate a fresh random IV per record and treat decryption failures as tampering.
Cookie encryption keys face the same lifecycle problem as signing keys: a per-instance or per-restart key invalidates sessions, and rotation must read old records.
The serialized record still must fit the ~4 KB cookie limit, and the base64url form inflates it by a third.
